:::note[Status]
This section documents the UI-kit specification (`docs/design/UI-KITS.md`) the kits are being
rebuilt to. The [Node terminal kit](/docs/build/ui/frameworks/terminal-node/) is the first to ship

:::

Every Polaris Key SDK that draws UI is getting a **UI kit** built to one specification,
`docs/design/UI-KITS.md`: the screens a product needs to gate itself on a license, from boot and
sign-in to devices, updates and settings. The kits will share one component catalog, one theme
API, one copy catalog and one set of flows, so a person who moves between a product's app, the
customer portal and the console meets one system, whichever SDK the product links.

This section is the shared half of the kit docs. Each kit adds its own framework page, and its tab
on every component page, as it ships. Until a kit has its framework page, its current docs are on
its SDK page (see [The kits](#the-kits)).

## Two ways to integrate

- **The hosted card.** No UI code: the kit's sign-in form runs with `presentation: "browser"` and
  hands the whole flow to the Polaris Key sign-in card in the browser.
- **The kit.** The kit's own form, dropped in whole or used piece by piece, or your own UI drawn
  over the kit's headless layer and the SDK's primitives.

## Three layers in every kit

Every component in the [catalog](/docs/build/ui/components/) is specified in three layers, so a team can
drop in a flow, restyle a component, or rebuild the UI on the state alone:

- **(a) The drop-in flow:** one call that gates the app and runs every screen it needs.
- **(b) The styled parts:** each screen and each part on its own, themed, with slots.
- **(c) Headless:** the state machine, its actions and its copy keys, with no UI.

The specification names each layer per kit as follows; a kit's framework page documents the API it
ships.

| Kit     | (a) Drop-in flow                             | (b) Styled parts                                        | (c) Headless                                       |
| ------- | -------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| Web     | `<PolarisKeyGate>`, `<pk-gate>`              | `<Activate>`, `<DeviceList>` with `data-part` and slots | `useActivate()` (React), `ActivateModel` (ui-core) |
| SwiftUI | `.polarisKeyGate(client)`                    | `ActivateView`, `DeviceList` with a style               | `@Observable ActivateModel`                        |
| Compose | `PolarisKeyGate(client) { }`                 | `Activate(state)`, `DeviceList(state)` with `*Defaults` | `rememberActivateState(client)`                    |
| Godot   | `PKeyGate` node, `await PolarisKey.boot()`   | `PKeyActivate.tscn` with theme type variations          | `PKeyActivateController`                           |
| Qt      | `polaris_key.ui.qt.run_gate(client, window)` | `Activate.qml`, QWidget parts with QSS                  | `ActivateViewModel` (`polaris_key.ui.core`)        |

Layer (c) is to be one state machine in every language, specified once as shared fixtures: a
React screen, a SwiftUI screen and a Godot scene fed the same inputs will show the same step with
the same copy key. An app that draws its own UI on the SDK primitives gets the same steps, states
and copy keys as the drop-in.

## The look

- **The Polaris Key look by default.** Every kit is to render the brand's surface, text, status and
  elevation tokens, Rubik, and the radius and motion tokens. It is dark first with full light
  parity and a System, Dark and Light choice. Games and TV default to dark.
- **In the product's accent.** Polaris violet appears only when the integrator asks for
  `accent: "core"`. Every accent goes through one contrast resolver, so buttons, links and the
  focus ring stay legible in both themes ([Theming](/docs/build/ui/theming/#the-accent-resolver)).
- **In each platform's idiom.** The modern web flow card; Liquid Glass on Apple's 26 releases,
  with a designed fallback on the 18-era floor; Material 3 Expressive on Android; Fluent 2 on
  Windows; libadwaita on GNOME; modern game UI in Godot; a 2026 command line in the terminal.
  The product-first hierarchy, Rubik, the token colours, the copy and the flows stay identical
  everywhere.
- **Or the host's look.** The `native` preset keeps the structure, flows, copy and spacing and
  hands colour, type and materials to the host ([Theming](/docs/build/ui/theming/#the-native-preset)).

The specification's hard rules for a modern UI (no boxed forms, no heavy borders, no stock
alerts or spinners, visible states, tokenised motion) are checked by `pnpm ui:lint` and by each
kit's own tests.

## Product identity

The product is the hero of every kit screen. Polaris Key supplies the design language, structure
and polish; the product's name, icon and accent lead.

A kit's `ProductIdentity` holds `name`, `icon`, `developer`, and optionally `shortName`, `accent`,
`art`, `wordmark` and `deviceCodeUrl`. The kit fills it from, in order:

1. the integrator's theme (`product`);
2. the product's **registered presentation**: the `presentation` block of `.pkey/product`
   ([Presentation](/docs/build/manifest/authoring/#presentation-presentation)), served in the
   discovery document and read, verified and cached by the SDK;
3. the app bundle: `Info.plist`, the Android manifest, `package.json`'s `productName`, or
   Godot's `application/config/name` and icon.

Kits never fetch discovery or the icon themselves: they are to read the presentation through
their SDK, and fall through to the bundle until the SDK exposes it. With no icon at all, a kit draws a
monogram tile (the product's initial on a neutral surface), never a Polaris Key mark.

The accent follows the same idea: the integrator's colour, else the presentation's `accent` (its
`accentDark` in the dark scheme), else a colour derived from the product icon, else a neutral ink
primary.

Polaris Key itself appears only in the optional "Powered by Polaris Key" line or badge
(`poweredBy`, off by default), and in two statements that are true about who handles a step: the
sign-in footnote, and the device-code URL when the product sets no `deviceCodeUrl`. The six service
accents are off on product screens; an integrator can opt in with `serviceCues: true`.

## The presentation default

The specification gives every kit **one sign-in form**. Its body morphs in place through Sign in, Finish in your
browser (or the code), Choose a license (and Replace a device, when the license is full), and
Done. No sheet or dialog stacks on it. Activation with a license key is a step of the same form,
and also ships on its own for a key-only product.

One option sets where the form appears, with the same values in every kit:

| `presentation`       | The form                                                                                                                  |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `"inline"` (default) | In the screen or window pane the kit already owns                                                                         |
| `"sheet"`            | In one platform sheet or dialog that holds every step: a sheet on macOS, `ContentDialog` on Windows, `AdwDialog` on GNOME |
| `"browser"`          | The hosted sign-in card in the browser; the kit waits and moves on by itself                                              |

`replace` (`"inline"` or `"browser"`) does the same for Replace a device. Native controls stay
native inside the form, including the system confirmation for a destructive Replace where the
platform expects one.

## Accessibility

Every kit is to meet WCAG 2.2 AA in both themes, and the specification's shared rules: one heading per
screen; visible labels on every field; errors announced and focused; modals that trap focus,
restore it and close on Escape, B or back; layouts that survive the largest text size; full
keyboard, gamepad and D-pad reach; named icon-only controls; status never shown by colour alone;
the focus ring on keyboard focus only for pointer users, and always for gamepad and TV; and glass
that turns opaque under reduced transparency.

## The kits

The must kits ship first; the should kits follow the kit they extend.

## Writing into this section

A kit that ships adds, in its own change:

- **its framework page**, `build/ui/frameworks/<id>.mdx`, copied from the
  [framework page template](/docs/build/ui/frameworks/#the-framework-page-template);
- **its tab on each component page** it implements, in the page's "In each kit" section (the
  [component page template](/docs/build/ui/components/#the-component-page-template) shows the
  shape);
- **its baselines**, which appear on the component pages by themselves once the kit's files are
  named `<component>-<state>-<theme>.png` and its docs pattern in
  `packages/docs/src/lib/baselines.ts` selects one render per state and theme;
- **its sample**, under `examples/ui/<id>/`, with a row in `examples/ui/README.md`;
- **a slimmer README**: install, the one-line flow, and a link to its framework page.
